subject: to speed up drawing using other comptuer's resource?

messages.author: fd401050309efe36
messages.subject: to speed up drawing using other comptuer's resource?
parts:
Complete newbie. I am making a list of 11 graphs, each graph takes 4 hour to draw on my laptop, so I "outsource" it to the workstation in-office using makePSOCKcluster:

Solution 1:

parLapply(cl, data, function(x) {
    library(ggplot2);
    postscript(horizontal=T, file="Rarray.ps");
    print(ggplot(x, aes(x=timestamp, y=volume, fill=profit_threshold)) + geom_area());
    dev.off();
})

Problem being, the resulting file is also on the workstation. I'll have to copy them back to my laptop each time. And, if I use mutiple nodes on the workstation, they may all attempt to write to the same file and conflict.

Solution 2:

graphs <- parLapply(cl, data, function(x) {
    library(ggplot2);
    ggplot(x, aes(x=timestamp, y=volume, fill=profit_threshold)) + geom_area()
})
postscript(horizontal=T, file="Rarray.ps");
lapply(graphs, print)
dev.off()

Result: the workstation didn't labour at all, all CPU-intense operation are in print() locally, and was carried out on my laptop.

The profect solution would be to leave the making of the graph on the server, and output the graph locally. That would requrie asundering print(). Is there a way to do so?

Or, perhaps I should ask the other question: what can I do to reduce the time needed to make a graph? The same graphs, that takes 4 hour to draw each, only need seconds, if using R's native plot function; but R didn't provide the graphics features I need. Maybe I should sample my data down (my .Rdata is about 15MB), and take the learning curve of how to sample down without losing data characteristics (I am a total start in statistics).

Or, perhaps there is a version of ggplot2 to take advantage of multi-processor / core; I can quadruple the process with it. Drawing with GPU is probably not in my effort's reach.

Thanks in advance!

messages.author: 373beb702917b8b5
messages.subject: Re: to speed up drawing using other comptuer's resource?
parts:
Hi,

## creating the plot specification is relatively fast

system.time({
p <- ggplot(diamonds,
aes(x=carat, y=price, color=cut)) +
geom_point() +
geom_smooth(method = "loess") +
facet_wrap(~clarity, ncol=2)
})

## constructing the actual display is slow
system.time(print(p))


## we can do the slow part and save the results
system.time({
pgt <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p))
})

## now creating the actual plot is fast(er)
system.time(plot(pgt))

## This suggests that you should try

graphs <- parLapply(cl, data, function(x) {
library(ggplot2);

ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(ggplot(x, aes(x=timestamp, y=volume,
fill=profit_threshold)) + geom_area()))

})
postscript(horizontal=T, file="Rarray.ps");

lapply(graphs, plot)
dev.off()

Best,
Ista

parts: Thanks. Your answer is superb clear and in good style!

On Mon, 23 Sep 2013, Ista Zahn wrote:

> ## we can do the slow part and save the results
> system.time({
> pgt <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p))
> })

I have ggplot_build but not ggplot_gtable on my ggplot2 0.8.9.
Although I do find a manual for ggplot_gtable:
RSiteSearch("ggplot_gtable")

I tried to put the return value of ggplot_build directly into plot() and
failed. Do I have to upgrade?

> ## now creating the actual plot is fast(er)
> system.time(plot(pgt))

I am trying to resolve why, a data frame of 9MB in size - as reported by
object.size() - takes 4 hours to area-chart; and how to speed it up.

And that "plot(pgt)" came as a surprise. Does ggplot2 use base plot() for
underlying graph even without explicit use of ggplot_gtable? If so, there
should be a performance penalty when ggplot2 overdo plot(), like
area-filling, when plot() at best does line-charts. So, I replaced
geom_area() with geom_line() for a test. The result: oops, instead of 4
hours, I got a graph in a minute!

So, if I still do most of my work on a laptop, there seems to be two exits
for me: either try to represent the data in ways other than area charts,
i.e. geom_area(), or, look for a package not using plot() for area charts
e.g. using filled.contour() or its own graphic devices...

Yes, I believe so. I'm not sure, but I think ggplot_gtable was
introduced somewhere around version 0.9.

>
>
>> ## now creating the actual plot is fast(er)
>> system.time(plot(pgt))
>
>
> I am trying to resolve why, a data frame of 9MB in size - as reported by
> object.size() - takes 4 hours to area-chart; and how to speed it up.

Well, it's not just an area chart, it's a stacked area chart, so it
has to figure out the min and max values.

>
> And that "plot(pgt)" came as a surprise. Does ggplot2 use base plot() for
> underlying graph even without explicit use of ggplot_gtable?

No, that's not the way R works. plot() does different things depending
on the class of it's argument.

If so, there
> should be a performance penalty when ggplot2 overdo plot(), like
> area-filling, when plot() at best does line-charts.
No, see above.

So, I replaced
> geom_area() with geom_line() for a test. The result: oops, instead of 4
> hours, I got a graph in a minute!
Yes, the area geom is slow.

>
> So, if I still do most of my work on a laptop, there seems to be two exits
> for me: either try to represent the data in ways other than area charts,
> i.e. geom_area(), or, look for a package not using plot() for area charts
> e.g. using filled.contour() or its own graphic devices...

You can certainly try to find a package that allows you to create this
graphic in less time, but avoiding plot() has nothing to do with it.
Actually if I were you I would probably reduce the granularity of the
data before plotting, e.g., averaging across every 100 values or so
(depending on the number of rows...)

Best,
Ista

the concept is interesting, I need some time for homework.

I did googled 20 minutes for alternative ways to plot area charts. No, not
any other visualization package offer this type of commonly-seen chart. It
seems to suggest, although a favourite toy of financial officers, area
charts are not popular in statistician circle at all, which behoove me to
study statistical charting. I may be more exposed to this difference by
working on financial statistics.

The reason I use area chart instead of line chart at the outset, is that my
data volatiles. A line chart is just a dense drop of ink, not to mention
compare several lines - while each line is always above/higher than another,
the characteristics are not identifiable.
